blocks.text: The paratonsillar vein is a major venous drainage pathway of the palatine tonsils and is vulnerable to injury during tonsillectomy. Profuse post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage, especially after surgery, commonly results from the rupture of this vein, leading to continuous bleeding.

Secondary supply to the pharynx & tonsils

blocks.text: **Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (Option A):** Incorrect because while it supplies the tonsil, arterial bleeding is less common post-tonsillectomy compared to venous bleeding.
**Ascending pharyngeal artery (Option B):** Incorrect because it primarily supplies the pharynx but is not the major source of post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage.
**Retromandibular vein (Option D):** Incorrect because it drains the face and has no direct relation to the tonsils.
The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle is the only abductor of the vocal cords. It pulls the arytenoid cartilages laterally, opening the glottis and allowing air passage during respiration.

blocks.title: Muscles of the Larynx
rows: Only abductor, opens airway during inspiration.

blocks.text: **Lateral cricoarytenoid (Option A):** Incorrect because it adducts the vocal cords, closing the glottis.
**Thyroarytenoid (Option C):** Incorrect because it relaxes the vocal cords, reducing tension.
**Vocalis (Option D):** Incorrect because it tenses the vocal cords, adjusting voice pitch.

The thyroid cartilage is an unpaired cartilage of the larynx, forming the Adam’s apple. It is the largest laryngeal cartilage and consists of two laminae fused in the midline. Unlike the other options, which exist as pairs, the thyroid cartilage is singular.

rows: Forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam’s apple), provides structural support.
Complete ring, supports larynx, attachment site for muscles.
Leaf-shaped, prevents food from entering the trachea.
Sits on top of arytenoids, helps with voice modulation.
Provides structural support to the laryngeal inlet.

blocks.text: **Arytenoid cartilage (Option A):** Incorrect because it is paired, playing a key role in vocal cord movement.
**Cuneiform cartilage (Option C):** Incorrect because it is paired, embedded in the aryepiglottic folds for support.
**Corniculate cartilage (Option D):** Incorrect because it is paired, sitting atop the arytenoids to assist in voice modulation.

The epiglottis is composed of elastic cartilage, which does not undergo calcification with age. In contrast, cartilages made of hyaline cartilage - such as the thyroid, cricoid, and parts of the arytenoid cartilage - tend to calcify and ossify over time.

blocks.title: Laryngeal Cartilages and Aging Changes
rows: Provides structural support to the airway
Hyaline (except vocal process, which has elastic cartilage)

blocks.text: **Thyroid cartilage (Option A):** incorrect because it is composed of hyaline cartilage, which calcifies and ossifies with age.
**Arytenoid cartilage (Option B):** incorrect because it has both hyaline and elastic components. The hyaline part calcifies, but the elastic part (vocal process) does not.
**Cricoid cartilage (Option D):** incorrect because it is made of hyaline cartilage, which undergoes calcification over time.

Killian’s dehiscence is a potential weak area in the posterior pharyngeal wall, located between the cricopharyngeus (inferior part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor) and thyropharyngeus (superior part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor). This site is prone to the formation of Zenker’s diverticulum, a pharyngeal pouch due to increased pressure during swallowing.

blocks.title: Pharyngeal Muscles and Weak Areas
rows: Forms upper boundary of Killian's dehiscence
Forms lower boundary of Killian's dehiscence

blocks.text: **Palatopharyngeus and Cricopharyngeus (Option A):** Incorrect because palatopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle of the pharynx, unrelated to Killian’s dehiscence.
**Thyropharyngeus and Palatopharyngeus (Option B):** Incorrect because palatopharyngeus is not involved in this weak area.
**Palatopharyngeus and Salpingopharyngeus (Option D):** Incorrect as these muscles are involved in pharyngeal elevation, not the formation of Killian’s dehiscence.

The Genioglossus muscle is fan-shaped and extends from the mandible to the tongue. The direction of fibers in the image indicates a broad origin from the mandible and insertion into the tongue. Function: It protrudes the tongue (helps in sticking out the tongue).
**Hyoglossus (Option B):** Incorrect because it arises from the hyoid bone and functions in tongue depression.
**Styloglossus (Option C):** Incorrect because it originates from the styloid process and functions in tongue retraction.
**Palatoglossus (Option D):** Incorrect because it arises from the soft palate and functions in elevating the tongue.

The marked structure is located posteriorly in the trachea, bridging the open ends of the C-shaped tracheal cartilage rings. This is the trachealis muscle, a smooth muscle that allows flexibility during swallowing and coughing.

blocks.title: Tracheal Structure
rows: Regulates tracheal diameter, aids in forceful expiration

blocks.text: **Tracheal cartilage (Option B):** Incorrect because the marked structure is soft muscle, whereas cartilage forms the rigid anterior C-shaped rings.
**Esophageal submucosal gland (Option C):** Incorrect because the structure is within the trachea, not the esophagus.
**Perichondrium (Option D):** Incorrect because the perichondrium is the fibrous layer covering the tracheal cartilage, not the posterior muscle.

items.text: **A (Posterior belly of digastric):** Facial nerve
**B (Anterior belly of digastric):** Mandibular nerve

blocks.text: Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Option A - A - Nerve to mylohyoid, B- Facial nerve:** This incorrectly swaps the nerves; the posterior belly is innervated by the facial nerve, not the nerve to mylohyoid.
**Option B - A - Facial nerve, B- Spinal accessory nerve:** The spinal accessory nerve does not supply the anterior belly of digastric but innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
**Option D - A - Spinal accessory nerve, B- Mandibular nerve:** The posterior belly is not supplied by the spinal accessory nerve but by the facial nerve.

blocks.text: The jugular foramen, located at the base of the skull, transmits several cranial nerves and venous structures; however, the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) does not pass through it, as it exits the skull via the hypoglossal canal situated medial and anterior to the foramen.

blocks.text: Frey’s syndrome (also called gustatory sweating) occurs when a patient sweats and flushes over the parotid (preauricular) region during eating or thinking about food.

**Mechanism after parotidectomy:** During surgery, the auriculotemporal nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve, CN V3) is often injured. This nerve carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland and sympathetic fibres to sweat glands.

After nerve injury, aberrant regeneration occurs: Parasympathetic fibres (originally meant for salivary secretion) regrow and mistakenly connect to sweat glands of the overlying skin. When eating stimulates salivation, these sweat glands are also activated, causing redness and sweating in that region.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Horner’s syndrome (Option B):** Triad: Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on the same side of the face due to sympathetic pathway lesion. Here, sweating is increased, not decreased, and there’s no mention of eye signs.
**Bell’s palsy (Option C):** Lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy: unilateral facial muscle weakness, inability to close the eye, drooping mouth. No sweating/redness triggered by eating.
**Glossopharyngeal neuralgia (Option D):** Severe paroxysmal pain in the throat, tonsillar fossa, and ear due to CN IX irritation. Pain, not sweating, is the main feature.

blocks.text: Superior orbital fissure syndrome compresses cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and VI, causing ophthalmoplegia and ptosis due to impaired eye movement and sensory loss around the eye.
Superior orbital fissure: Triangular gap through which the middle cranial fossa connects with the orbit

blocks.text: V2 (maxillary nerve) and II (optic nerve) (Option B, C, D) do not pass through the superior orbital fissure: V2 passes through the foramen rotundum. II passes through the optic canal.

The uncinate process is a thin, curved bony structure of the ethmoid bone that extends superiorly and typically attaches to the middle nasal concha (middle turbinate), helping to form part of the lateral nasal wall and the drainage pathway of the frontal sinus.
**Components of the Middle Meatus of the Nose:**

items.text: **Uncinate Process:** Hook-like structure running from anterosuperior to posteroinferior. Forms a gap with the bulla ethmoidalis called the hiatus semilunaris inferior. Divides the lower middle meatus into anterior and posterior fontanelles (membranous areas).
**Infundibulum:** Bounded medially by the uncinate process and laterally by the lamina papyracea. Contains the natural ostium of the maxillary sinus in its lower part.
**Bulla Ethmoidalis:** Ethmoidal cell located behind the uncinate process, forming the posterior boundary of the hiatus semilunaris. May be pneumatized or a solid prominence.
**Hiatus Semilunaris:** Inferior: The gap between the uncinate process and bulla. Superior: The cleft between the bulla and skull base.
**Ostiomeatal Unit (Complex):** Key area where the ostia of the frontal, ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses drain into the middle meatus. Common drainage pathway for the anterior group of sinuses.

blocks.text: Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Superior turbinate (Option B):** The uncinate process does not attach here; it is located lower than the superior turbinate.
**Inferior turbinate (Option C):** This is a separate bone and much lower in the nasal cavity, so the uncinate process doesn’t attach to it.
**Bulla ethmoidalis (Option D):** This is a separate ethmoid air cell located posterior to the uncinate process, not an attachment site.

blocks.text: In adults, the glottis- specifically the rima glottidis, the space between the true vocal cords - is the narrowest part of the laryngeal airway and plays a key role in controlling airflow and voice production.
Incorrect Options:

items.text: **Supraglottic region (Option A)** includes the structures above the vocal cords (like the epiglottis and false vocal cords), and it is wider than the glottis.
**Subglottic region (Option C):** is located below the vocal cords; it's wider than the glottis in adults but is the narrowest part in children.
**Trachea (Option D):** is significantly wider than the glottis.

blocks.text: The fishbone is impacted at the T4 level, where the aortic arch crosses the esophagus and creates a normal anatomical narrowing, making it the most likely site of obstruction.
Oesophageal Constrictions: Constrictions occur at four main points:

rows: This first constriction is at the upper esophageal sphincter where the esophagus begins. It is caused by the cricopharyngeus muscle, which plays a role in swallowing.
The second narrowing occurs where the arch of the aorta crosses the esophagus. The pressure from the aorta causes this indentation.
Left Main Bronchus (Option A ruled out)
Third constriction is where the left bronchus crosses over the esophagus, leading to a narrowing.
The final narrowing happens where the esophagus passes through the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus.

blocks.text: The arrow likely points to the posterior cranial fossa, specifically the tentorium cerebelli (a dural fold), as this area is clinically significant for referred pain. The dura mater in the posterior cranial fossa (innervated by the meningeal branches of the upper cervical nerves, particularly C1-C3) refers pain to the occipital region (back of the head) and neck.
This is because the sensory innervation of the dura in this region shares spinal cord segments (C1-C3) with cutaneous nerves supplying the occiput and neck, leading to referred pain in these areas.
Referred pain sites:

items.text: **Vertex (Option B):** Pain from supratentorial dura (innervated by the trigeminal nerve, V1-V3).
**Ear (Option C):** Middle cranial fossa dura (trigeminal or glossopharyngeal innervation).
**Shoulder (Option D):** Lower cervical dura (C4-C5), not typical for posterior fossa.

blocks.text: The marked structure is the dorsal aspect of the brainstem, specifically the region of the midbrain, near the inferior colliculus. Cranial Nerve IV (Trochlear Nerve) is the only cranial nerve that emerges from the dorsal aspect of the brainstem. The trochlear nerve decussates (crosses) before exiting, meaning a lesion in one trochlear nucleus affects the contralateral superior oblique muscle.
**Function:** It innervates the superior oblique muscle, aiding in intorsion and depression of the eye in adduction.

blocks.title: Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) and its Unique Features
rows: Dorsal midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus
Only cranial nerve to exit dorsally
Crosses completely before exiting, affecting the contralateral superior oblique muscle
Vertical diplopia (trouble looking down, especially while reading or descending stairs)

blocks.text: **Cranial Nerve III (Option A):** Incorrect because CN III emerges from the ventral midbrain (interpeduncular fossa), not the dorsal brainstem.
**Cranial Nerve V (Option B):** Incorrect because CN V emerges from the pons, not the dorsal aspect of the brainstem.
**Cranial Nerve VI (Option D):** Incorrect because CN VI emerges from the pontomedullary junction (ventral side), not dorsally.

The levator scapulae muscle is primarily innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5), with additional contributions from C3 and C4 spinal nerves. The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root of the brachial plexus and also supplies the rhomboid major and minor muscles. Function: Elevates the scapula and assists in downward rotation.

items.text: **Suprascapular nerve (option B):** Innervates supraspinatus and infraspinatus, not the levator scapulae. Arises from the upper trunk (C5-C6) of the brachial plexus.
**From the dorsal rami of C1 (option C):** C1 dorsal ramus contributes to the suboccipital nerve, which innervates suboccipital muscles, not the levator scapulae.
**Subscapular nerve (option D):** The upper and lower subscapular nerves (from C5-C6) supply the subscapularis and teres major, not the levator scapulae.
